title: Web Search Engine
summary: Design the indexing and query-serving stack of a web search engine over billions of documents.
statement: Design a web search engine. Given crawled pages, build an index, then serve queries with relevant ranked results in a few hundred milliseconds. Cover index construction, distribution, ranking, and freshness. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.
coreFunctionalRequirements: Build an inverted index from crawled documents.
Answer text queries with ranked results.

requirementQuestions.question: How many documents, queries per second, and what index size?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: What query latency is expected at p99?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Defines which paths need caching, precomputation, or regional placement.

requirementQuestions.question: How fresh must the index be for news versus the long tail?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Selects between strong and eventual models and shapes conflict handling.

requirementQuestions.question: Which ranking signals (links, quality, personalisation) are included?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

requirementQuestions.question: What happens when some index shards are unavailable?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

requirementQuestions.question: How is the hardware cost of the index managed?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Prevents over-engineering and affects build-versus-buy choices.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: How many shards and replicas does the index need?
How many shards does each query touch?
What is the update volume per day?

keyDecisions.question: How is the index organised?
considerations: Inverted index with compressed posting lists.
Partition by document (each shard holds a subset) for parallel queries.
Tiered indexes: fresh, high-quality, long tail.

keyDecisions.question: How are queries answered?
considerations: Broadcast to shards, each returns top results, then merge.
Early termination and caching of popular queries.
Replicas for throughput and tail latency.

keyDecisions.question: How are results ranked?
considerations: First-pass scoring (BM25) then machine-learned reranking of top candidates.

keyDecisions.question: How are documents processed?
considerations: Parse, tokenise, dedupe, and score documents offline in batches.

keyDecisions.question: How does it handle failures?
considerations: Replicas and tolerant merging with partial results.
Graceful degradation by skipping slow shards.
Canary rollouts of new index versions.

tradeoffs.tension: Parallelism and simplicity versus per-term locality.
More reranking improves quality but adds time.

commonMistakes: Using a general-purpose database for text search.
Querying every shard with no caching or early termination.
No tiering, so the long tail dominates cost.
Ignoring tail latency from slow shards.
followUps: How do you handle spam and low-quality pages?
How would you add a news freshness tier?
How do you evaluate ranking changes?
How do you serve multiple languages?
